traveler: Max Perelman (Max Perlman, born Meiers Perlmanis)
title: S'iz nisht dos vos amol iz geven: the Riga Choirboy, the Excelsior, and the Hat Used as a Prop
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Riga: The Cantor's Choir and the Peretz Club

stops.name: Riga, birth in the Jewish quarter
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by Belling and independently by Wikidata Q81939428 (with VIAF 98494469 and LC no2019073077). No source located gives the day, the month, or the birth address; the date is defaulted to 1 January for ordering only, and the pin marks the Old Town Jewish quarter, not a house.
stops.campa: In Riga a son is born into a middle-class Jewish family and entered on the register as Meiers Perlmanis. The city carries one of the densest Yiddish-speaking populations of the Baltic: its own press, its own schools, its own long quarrel over whether Yiddish is a language or a jargon. Nothing survives in reach of the day, the month, the street, or the names of his parents. The register holds a year, 1909, and the surname Perlmanis. It will be printed as Perlman, Perelman and Perlmann on playbills across four continents before he is done with it.
suggested_refs: The Jewish quarter of Riga's Old Town, birthplace of a name later spelled Perlman, Perelman, Perlmann and Perlmanis
sources: Veronica Belling, 'S'iz nisht dos vos amol iz geven: Max Perlman (1909-1985),' Digital Yiddish Theatre Project, 2020

stops.name: Riga, the choir of Cantor Rozovski
stops.date_confidence: Belling gives only 'about age six', which places this around 1915; the month and day are invented for ordering. The cantor is named in the source but his synagogue is not, so the pin repeats the Old Town quarter.
stops.campa: At about six he is put into the choir of Cantor Rozovski and learns to carry a line in front of a congregation before he can read a score. Children's parts in the Yiddish theatre follow almost at once. Two trainings start in the same year and never afterward separate in him: the liturgical voice, pitched to reach the back of a room without amplification, and the stage child's early arithmetic of what an audience will laugh at and how soon. Which synagogue held the choir, no source consulted says.
suggested_refs: The cantorial choir tradition of Riga, first training of the Yiddish stage's comic tenors

stops.name: Riga, the dramatic studio of the Peretz Club
stops.date_confidence: Belling dates this only to the 1920s; 1925 is a midpoint chosen for ordering. The Peretz Club building could not be located in any source reached. An earlier draft placed the pin in the Maskavas forstate, Riga's Moscow suburb, at 56.9375, 24.1418; that coordinate is not supported and the Old Town pin is used instead, with the district claim dropped.
stops.campa: He enrolls in the dramatic studio of the Peretz Club, named for I. L. Peretz, and takes the training a serious young Riga actor takes: Russian repertoire and Yiddish repertoire, both, in the same rooms, from the same teachers. He performs in both languages from the start. The studio hands him a reflex rather than a style: two tongues held at once, and the choice between them made line by line. Thirty years on the Russian will be Spanish and the slang will come off the streets of Buenos Aires. Where the Peretz Club kept its rooms has not been established in any source reached.
suggested_refs: The Riga Peretz Club, seedbed of interwar Latvian Yiddish acting

stops.name: Riga, the Nayer Yidisher Teater and the turn professional
stops.date_confidence: Belling gives 1928 as the start of the professional career with the New Yiddish Theatre of Riga; month and day unrecorded. The UBA dictionary independently frames the Riga and Kovno phase as running 'desde 1928 a 1934'.
stops.campa: The New Yiddish Theatre opens in Riga and takes him on, and at nineteen he is a professional. For six years the work runs along one rail, Riga to Kovno and back, through operetta, melodrama, and the sketch comedy that turns out to be his actual trade. Nobody outside the Baltic knows the name yet. He is learning to work rooms where the audience answers back, and learning that he does not mind wanting to be liked. Belling puts the start of the professional career in 1928. The month is not recorded anywhere.
suggested_refs: The Nayer Yidisher Teater of Riga, founded 1928
sources: Glocer et al., Diccionario biografico y bibliografico de musicos judios exiliados en Argentina, vol. II, p. 156

stops.name: Kaunas, the other end of the Baltic circuit
stops.date_confidence: The Kovno engagements fall inside the attested 1928-1934 span; the specific year is chosen for ordering. No theatre in Kaunas is named in any source consulted, so the pin is city-level.
stops.campa: Kovno, capital of independent Lithuania, is the second pole of the circuit, two hundred miles from Riga across a border younger than he is, and for six years he shuttles between the two cities as the seasons demand. Yiddish theatre in the Baltic republics is not a subsidised art in these years; it is a business of tours, split takes, and halls booked for a fortnight. He learns the economics along with the repertoire. No hall in Kovno is named for him in anything reachable. The record gives two cities and six years and stops there.
suggested_refs: The interwar Yiddish theatre circuit of Kaunas and Riga
sources: Glocer et al., Diccionario, vol. II, p. 156

segments.name: Gita Galina and the European Circuit

stops.name: Riga, meeting Gita Galina
stops.date_confidence: Belling places the meeting in the Riga theatre without a year; 1932 is inferred from the fact that the joint touring begins before the 1934-35 London engagement. Galina's own record (Wikidata Q81939577, following the UBA dictionary) gives her birth as circa 1907 in Vitebsk under the name Guta Israiley.
stops.campa: In the Riga theatre he meets Guita Galina, born Guta Israiley in Vitebsk two years before him and already the more established of the two. They marry and they tour, and from this point the record almost never names one without the other: the same companies, the same playbills, the same steamer tickets, for close to half a century. She plays the ingenue to his shlemazl. When she is too old for ingenues, and only then, does another actress take those parts, and Galina keeps working beside him anyway.
suggested_refs: Gita Galina, born Guta Israiley, Vitebsk c. 1907
sources: Glocer et al., Diccionario, vol. I, p. 195

stops.name: Vienna, the Central European tour
stops.date_confidence: The UBA dictionary lists the tour as 'Viena, Checoslovaquia, Polonia, Francia, Belgica e Inglaterra' with no dates at all; Belling says the 1930s. The year is an ordering guess bounded by the 1934 close of the Baltic phase and the 1935 closure of the London Pavilion.
stops.campa: The pair leave the Baltic and work westward: Vienna, Czechoslovakia, a guest engagement with Poland's Skale company. It is the ordinary itinerary of a Yiddish touring act in the last years when that itinerary is still possible, city to city across a Europe whose Jewish theatres are all still open and all still full. He is in his mid-twenties and playing comedy. Within a decade most of these houses will not exist and most of these audiences will be dead. The reference work that lists the itinerary dates none of it: Vienna, Czechoslovakia, Poland, France, Belgium, England, in that order and nothing more.
suggested_refs: The Skale Theater of Poland, guest engagement of the mid-1930s
sources: Glocer et al., Diccionario, vol. II, p. 156

stops.name: Paris, a year of engagements
stops.date_confidence: Belling gives roughly a year in Paris and Belgium without dates; the year is placed here for ordering only. The coordinate is the pin used across the corpus for Paris.
stops.campa: A year, near enough, in Paris and across the Belgian border, playing to the Yiddish-speaking emigration of the west: Polish and Lithuanian Jews already one displacement into their lives, watching two Latvians perform the comedy of home. Belgium is folded into the same engagement in every source consulted, without a city named. He is working in his fourth country and his repertoire has not yet had to change. That comes later, and it comes in Spanish.
suggested_refs: The Yiddish theatres of interwar Paris and their emigre audiences
sources: Glocer et al., Diccionario, vol. II, p. 156

stops.name: Pavilion Theatre, Whitechapel Road, the London season
stops.date_confidence: Belling dates the London engagement loosely to the 1930s, but the Pavilion Theatre at 191-193 Whitechapel Road closed in 1935 and was cleared in 1962, so the visit cannot fall later than 1935 and most likely follows immediately on the 1934 close of the Riga and Kovno phase. Month and day are chosen for ordering. Coordinate taken from the Wikipedia and Survey of London records for the building, which sat behind the Whitechapel Road frontage.
stops.campa: The Pavilion on Whitechapel Road is the great Yiddish playhouse of the English-speaking world, a barn of a theatre in the middle of the East End, and he plays it with Galina. It has perhaps a year of life left in it. He is not yet thirty and he has already worked Riga, Paris and London. Belling puts the engagement loosely in the 1930s; the building narrows it, since the house shuts in 1935 and the site is cleared in 1962. Of all his stages this is the one datable by its own demolition.
suggested_refs: The Pavilion Theatre, 191-193 Whitechapel Road, closed 1935, demolished 1962; Survey of London feature 1468

stops.name: Manchester, the British provincial circuit
stops.date_confidence: Belling names Liverpool, Leeds, Manchester and Glasgow together without dates or venues; Manchester stands here for all four and the date orders the segment. No individual theatre is named in any source reached.
stops.campa: After London the regional tour: Liverpool, Leeds, Manchester, Glasgow, the four provincial cities where Britain's Jewish immigration settled thickest. These are one-night and one-week rooms, not seasons. He and Galina travel with the music parts and a repertoire cut down to what two people can carry between trains. The Jewish Chronicle, reviewing him somewhere in these British years, files the phrase that follows him for the rest of his working life and describes exactly the instrument he performs with.
stops.quote: with the friendliest smile on the Yiddish stage
stops.quote_source: Jewish Chronicle (London), undated review, quoted in Belling, Digital Yiddish Theatre Project, 2020
suggested_refs: The Jewish theatre audiences of Manchester, Leeds, Liverpool and Glasgow between the wars

stops.name: Warsaw, the shooting of Mamele
stops.date_confidence: The film is a 1938 release and the shoot is generally placed in the autumn of that year; the exact dates of his own days on set are not recorded anywhere consulted. Warsaw studios carried the main production, with exteriors at Lodz and Ciechocinek, but no source names him at the exterior locations. The pin is the corpus's Warsaw coordinate.
stops.campa: Joseph Green and Konrad Tom are shooting Mamele in and around Warsaw with Molly Picon in the title part, and he is cast as Dawid Samet. It is made in the last full year of Jewish Warsaw, and within four years the studios, the extras and most of the audience the picture was made for are gone. The film is the only surviving record of what he looked like working. The catalogue of the National Center for Jewish Film still lists him by the screen spelling, Max Perelman. Exteriors were shot at Lodz and Ciechocinek; no source places him at either.
suggested_refs: Mamele (1938), dir. Joseph Green and Konrad Tom, with Molly Picon; National Center for Jewish Film print
sources: National Center for Jewish Film catalogue, 'Mamele'

segments.name: The Oceania: Buenos Aires and the Compania Israelita de Operetas

stops.name: Trieste, the embarkation for the River Plate
stops.date_confidence: The UBA dictionary states that on 7 June 1939 he ARRIVED in Argentina with Gita Galina aboard the Oceania, 'habiendo embarcado en Trieste'. The embarkation itself is undated in the record; May 1939 is a placeholder that orders the crossing before the arrival. An earlier reading of this passage that treated 7 June as the departure date is wrong. Coordinate is the Stazione Marittima.
stops.campa: They board the Oceania at Trieste. Adolf Mide has invited them to Buenos Aires for an engagement, and an engagement is what they think they are taking. The port is by this date one of the working exits from Europe for Jews with papers and passage money, and the two of them have both. They will not see Riga again. Neither the manifest nor the ticket has been found in any archive consulted, and the day they sailed is not recorded either. The dictionary that attests the crossing gives only the arrival, 7 June 1939, and the phrase habiendo embarcado en Trieste.
suggested_refs: The Stazione Marittima at Trieste, embarkation point of the 1939 crossings
sources: Glocer et al., Diccionario, vol. II, p. 156
Glocer et al., Diccionario, vol. I, p. 195 (Galina)

stops.name: Port of Buenos Aires, the arrival of 7 June 1939
stops.date_confidence: Date attested to the day in the UBA dictionary, vol. II p. 156, and repeated for Galina at vol. I p. 195. The berth is not named; the pin is the corpus's port-of-Buenos-Aires coordinate.
stops.campa: The Oceania docks and two Latvian actors walk down onto a wharf in a city with more than a quarter of a million Jews in it, five professional Yiddish theatres, a Yiddish daily press, and a Jewish quarter that runs from Once through Villa Crespo. Three months later Germany invades Poland and the engagement becomes an address. Buenos Aires is where the rest of his life is organised from, whatever continent he happens to be working on, and he is thirty years old the week he arrives.
suggested_refs: The steamer Oceania, Trieste to Buenos Aires, arriving 7 June 1939
sources: Glocer et al., Diccionario, vol. II, p. 156

stops.name: Teatro Excelsior, Corrientes 3224, the three-year residency
stops.date_confidence: Belling gives roughly three years at the Excelsior from 1939; no opening date is recorded and September is chosen to order the stop. Address confirmed as Avenida Corrientes 3224, facing the old Abasto market, opened 1912 and demolished 1961; coordinate corrected to the OSM geocode of that address.
stops.campa: He joins the Compania Israelita de Operetas and becomes the headline attraction at the Excelsior on Corrientes, across from the Abasto market, for about three years. The commercial Yiddish houses of the city in these years are the Soleil, the Excelsior, the Ombu and the Mitre, with the independent IFT alongside them and Yiddish vaudeville running in the bars El Cristal and El Internacional. Into that circuit walks a comedian who already works in four languages and is about to start writing songs in a fifth. The Excelsior opened in 1912 and was demolished in 1961.
suggested_refs: Teatro Excelsior, Avenida Corrientes 3224, opened 1912, demolished 1961
sources: Teatros de Buenos Aires del Siglo XVII al XXI, '1912 Teatro Excelsior'
Digital Yiddish Theatre Project / Fordham, on the Buenos Aires Yiddish houses of the mid-1930s

stops.name: Teatro Excelsior, the JKG concert of 9 May 1942
stops.date_confidence: Date and personnel come from the UBA dictionary; the entry was not independently cross-checked against the Buenos Aires German-Jewish press for this stop, though the parallel 1943 entry was. Retained as attested on that single archival authority.
stops.campa: He appears with Galina at the Excelsior under the baton of Leo Schwarz, in a concert mounted by the Jewish cultural society of the German-speaking refugees. The date matters for a reason having nothing to do with music. In the same summer a different Max Perlman, an American relief administrator, is running the Joint Distribution Committee's operations out of North Africa and then Bari, and the two men have been confused ever since. On 9 May 1942 the singer is on a stage on Corrientes.
suggested_refs: The Judische Kulturgemeinschaft concerts of wartime Buenos Aires
sources: Glocer et al., Diccionario, vol. II, p. 156
Jewish Telegraphic Agency archive, 'Max Perlman Heads J.D.C. Office in Bari,' 2 July 1944 (the namesake)

stops.name: Salon Union Tranviarios, Rund um die Operette
stops.date_confidence: Date, venue, personnel and press notices are given in the UBA dictionary, vol. I p. 283, under the Horvath Sandor entry, with contemporary notices in Argentinisches Tageblatt, 1 July 1943 p. 4, and La Semana Israelita, 16 July 1943 p. 9. The street address of the Salon Union Tranviarios could not be established, so the pin falls back to the corpus's generic Buenos Aires coordinate.
stops.campa: In the tramworkers' union hall, the Sociedad Cultural Israelita puts on an evening of operetta by Jewish composers: Offenbach, Paul Abraham, Olshanetzky, Leo Fall, Kalman, Brodsky, Oscar Straus. Victor Schlichter conducts, Andre Laszlo directs, Horvath Sandor leads the gypsy orchestra, and the Compania Israelita contingent is Gita Galina, Max Perlmann and Philipp Wenning. Central Europe is being murdered as the programme is printed. The hall in Buenos Aires plays its music through.
suggested_refs: Programme of Rund um die Operette, Salon Union Tranviarios, 14 July 1943; Argentinisches Tageblatt, 1 July 1943
sources: Glocer et al., Diccionario, vol. I, p. 283
La Semana Israelita, year IV no. 170, 16 July 1943, p. 9

segments.name: The Southern Cone and the First South African Season

stops.name: Montevideo, the river crossed
stops.date_confidence: The UBA dictionary compresses this phase into one sentence, 'Hasta 1947 realizo espectaculos tambien en Brasil, Uruguay y Chile'; no year within that span is assigned to any one country and no venue is named. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: With the Excelsior residency behind him he works the regional circuit that Buenos Aires anchors, and the first leg of it is the shortest: across the Plate to Montevideo, where the Uruguayan Jewish community is small enough that a visiting company is an event and large enough to fill a hall. No theatre in Montevideo is named in anything reachable. He is thirty-five, and the language he was trained to perform in has just lost most of the people who spoke it. The phase runs five years, and its whole record is one clause in a reference work: Brazil, Uruguay and Chile, until 1947. Which halls, in which order, in which years?
suggested_refs: The Yiddish-speaking community of Montevideo in the 1940s
sources: Glocer et al., Diccionario, vol. II, p. 156

stops.name: Santiago de Chile, over the cordillera
stops.date_confidence: Within the attested 'hasta 1947' Southern Cone phase; the specific year orders the segment. No Chilean venue is identified in any source consulted.
stops.campa: Chile is the far end of the circuit, over the Andes, and the Jewish population there is smaller again, much of it arrived within the previous ten years from the same Central Europe he himself left in 1939. He plays to rooms of people whose displacement is more recent than his own. He does not bring them lament. He brings operetta, sketch comedy and songs about money, and Santiago hears the Buenos Aires repertoire as Buenos Aires hears it. No Chilean venue is identified in any source consulted, and no year inside the phase is assigned to Chile; 1945 orders the segment and claims nothing more than that.
suggested_refs: The refugee Jewish communities of Santiago in the 1940s
sources: Glocer et al., Diccionario, vol. II, p. 156

stops.name: Brazil, the northern leg
stops.date_confidence: The Brazilian leg of the 1940s Southern Cone phase is attested in the UBA dictionary, but no city is named there or anywhere else consulted. Sao Paulo is an inference from its standing as Brazil's principal Yiddish stage, not a documented location, and the coordinate should be read as reconstruction. A separate claim putting him in Brazil again in 1967 is unsupported and is not staged here.
stops.campa: Brazil closes the northern reach of the phase. Which city, the record does not say, and Sao Paulo is a guess made on the strength of its theatres rather than on any document, and the pin should be read as reconstruction. By 1947 the Southern Cone touring is finished. The audiences that made him in Europe are gone; the ones that will keep him for the next thirty-five years are in Argentina, South Africa, Israel and New York, and he has yet to set foot in three of the four. He is thirty-eight.
suggested_refs: The Yiddish stage of Sao Paulo, proposed but undocumented site of the 1940s Brazilian engagements
sources: Glocer et al., Diccionario, vol. II, p. 156

stops.name: His Majesty's Theatre, Johannesburg, the first South African season
stops.date_confidence: ESAT confirms he starred in Sarah Sylvia's season of Yiddish theatre at His Majesty's in 1948 with Guita Galina, but carries no run length and no attendance figures; the eight weeks and the twenty thousand in a fortnight are Belling's alone. Some accounts date the first season 1949. Coordinate corrected from the Johannesburg centroid to the artefacts.co.za record for the building at Commissioner, Eloff, Fox and Joubert Streets, Marshalltown.
stops.campa: Sarah Sylvia brings him to Johannesburg and he opens a musical revue at His Majesty's, in the theatre completed in 1945 after the war interrupted its building. Belling's account gives eight weeks and twenty thousand people through the doors in the first fortnight. The South African Jewish press promptly starts arguing about whether this is theatre at all, and a critic in Jewish Affairs sets out the three parties to the quarrel with more precision than anyone since.
stops.quote: First the so-called common man who goes to see light comedy because he likes light comedy, wants an evening's entertainment—and gets it. Secondly the group of kultur-menshn who go to see these light comedies in order to sneer and deride. They speak nostalgically about Great Yiddish Drama and sneak back again to gather more material for derision. The third group are the Super-Purists who have refrained from attending any of these performances, but loudly voice their disapproval. This, they say, is not Yiddish theatre.
stops.quote_source: A. Misheiker, Jewish Affairs 3, no. 12 (1948), 28-29, quoted in Belling, Digital Yiddish Theatre Project, 2020
suggested_refs: His Majesty's Theatre, Marshalltown, Johannesburg, completed 1945; artefacts.co.za building record 423
sources: Encyclopedia of South African Theatre (ESAT), 'Max Perlman'

stops.name: The Grand Palais, London, the first of three seasons
stops.date_confidence: Belling gives Grand Palais engagements in 1949, 1951 and 1955 without months. No source reached gives the theatre's coordinates, so the pin approximates the Commercial Road stretch of the East End Yiddish theatre district and should not be read as the building. The reviewing paper's date is likewise not fixed to one of the three seasons.
stops.campa: With the Pavilion long gone, the Grand Palais is what London's Yiddish theatre has left, and he plays it three times across six years: 1949, 1951, 1955. The Jewish East End is emptying northward through those same years and the audience thins as it goes. The Jewish Chronicle reviews him in the register the paper keeps for him throughout, mild about the play, delighted with the man, and clear-eyed that the two are not the same question. None of the three seasons can be told apart in the record, and the paper's own date is not fixed to any one of them.
stops.quote: It matters little that it is not very original or convincing, the important thing being its suitability as a vehicle for the antics of this most likeable comedian. He is a worm who turns, a shlemazzel who becomes successful, and the clowning, singing and dancing in which he indulges in the process are most entertaining. Guita Galina contributes some charming singing and playing as his wife.
stops.quote_source: Jewish Chronicle (London), review of one of the Grand Palais seasons of 1949, 1951 or 1955, quoted in Belling, Digital Yiddish Theatre Project, 2020
suggested_refs: The Grand Palais, Commercial Road, last of London's Yiddish playhouses

stops.name: Johannesburg, Menora Zahav at fifteen
stops.date_confidence: Belling dates the first Zahav performance to 1951 from interviews with Zahav herself on 24 and 25 December 2018; the venue is inferred from the same Johannesburg circuit rather than named for that year. Belling records South African tours in 1948/49, 1951 and 1972 and says he visited at least four times; a 1953 tour appears in some accounts but no source located supports it.
stops.campa: On the 1951 return an actress-singer of fifteen and a half performs with him for the first time in Johannesburg. Her name is Menora Zahav. She is a South African schoolgirl; he is a forty-two-year-old star out of Riga by way of Buenos Aires, and she will still be onstage with him thirty-four years later, on the last tour of his life. The oral history is her own, given to a researcher in 2018. Another man who sat in those South African houses as a boy wrote to the same researcher sixty years afterward, and what he remembered was not a play.
stops.quote: I loved Max Perlman... I loved the jaunty, cocksure persona that came across so vividly, nothing like the Yiddish speakers that I knew at the time, who were old, spoke bad English, and of whom I was a bit ashamed. He represented a confident and glorious Yiddish, risen from the Holocaust.
stops.quote_source: Bruce Oppenheimer, e-mail to Veronica Belling, 16 August 2018, quoted in Belling, Digital Yiddish Theatre Project, 2020
suggested_refs: Veronica Belling's 2018 interviews with Menora Zahav, 24-25 December 2018

segments.name: Ramat Gan, and the Circuit It Feeds

stops.name: United States, the first working visit
stops.date_confidence: The UBA dictionary states plainly: 'En 1952, fue a Estados Unidos, pais que alterno para trabajar con su hogar, en Israel.' No city is named, so the New York coordinate is an explicit placeholder and not a documented location. His first New York stage credits do not appear until 1962.
stops.campa: He goes to the United States to work for the first time. From here on the American engagements alternate with the Israeli home, in a pattern the reference books state without explaining. No city is recorded for 1952 and no production is attached to it; ten years will pass before his name appears on a New York playbill. The year opens the phase in which he works four continents at once, and the year rests on a single line in a Buenos Aires reference work: En 1952, fue a Estados Unidos, pais que alterno para trabajar con su hogar, en Israel.
suggested_refs: The 1952 American visit, recorded without a city in the UBA dictionary
sources: Glocer et al., Diccionario, vol. II, p. 157

stops.name: Israel, the grand debut and the nine-month season
stops.date_confidence: Belling dates the grand Israeli debut to 1954; the Jewish Chronicle notice of 8 January 1955 reports the visit as having run nine months, which places the season across 1954 into 1955. No opening venue is named, so the pin is the general Tel Aviv coordinate rather than a theatre.
stops.campa: He arrives in a state seven years old that has legislated against Yiddish performance in various ways and cannot stop its people going to see it. The season runs nine months. Hebrew is the official tongue of the country and the language of its national stage; the language of half its immigrants is the one he is selling, and he sells it as comedy rather than as mourning, which is the whole of his method and the reason the purists never forgive him.
stops.quote: Yiddish comedian 'conquered' Israel...Their nine month visit to the Jewish state was remarkable.
stops.quote_source: Jewish Chronicle, 8 January 1955, quoted in Belling, Digital Yiddish Theatre Project, 2020
suggested_refs: The Israeli Yiddish-language entertainment circuit of the 1950s, played against official Hebrew-only policy

stops.name: Ramat Gan, the mayor's ground-floor apartment
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The story comes from Menora Zahav's oral testimony to Belling in December 2018 and from nowhere else; no municipal record, deed or tenancy document has been examined by anyone in the chain. The date is chosen only to place the settling after the 1954-55 Israeli season.
stops.campa: Avraham Krinitzi, mayor of Ramat Gan, gives Max and Gita a small ground-floor apartment, and it becomes the only fixed home either of them keeps for the rest of their lives. Neither buys a house anywhere else, in five decades of working four continents. The whole of the evidence for the gift is an old woman's memory recorded in 2018: no deed, no tenancy record, no municipal file has been examined by anyone in the chain. The tours leave from here and come back to here, South Africa, Argentina, Britain, New York, Australia, and then a door at street level in Ramat Gan.
suggested_refs: The Ramat Gan apartment, attested only in Menora Zahav's 2018 oral testimony
sources: Belling, Digital Yiddish Theatre Project, 2020, citing Menora Zahav interviews of 24-25 December 2018

stops.name: Teatro Soleil, Buenos Aires, Der Amerikanische Littwak
stops.date_confidence: Date, title, director and cast come from the UBA dictionary; the street address of the Teatro Soleil could not be independently established, so the pin is the generic Buenos Aires coordinate. This is his first documented Soleil appearance, which is why the theatre does not belong in the early 1940s cluster where earlier accounts placed it.
stops.campa: Sixteen years after the Oceania docked he is back on a Buenos Aires stage, at the Soleil, in Der Amerikanische Littwak under Hermann Ludwig's direction with Galina beside him. Israel is the address now and Argentina is a place he returns to, in 1955 and again in 1966 and 1967. The play is a comedy about a Lithuanian who has become an American, performed in Buenos Aires by a Latvian, in Yiddish. The city does not treat him as a visitor; the same audience is in the seats. The date is 26 August 1955, and the Soleil's street address has not been established.
suggested_refs: Teatro Soleil, Buenos Aires, house of the Compania Israelita's later seasons
sources: Glocer et al., Diccionario, vol. II, p. 157

stops.name: Cape Town, the cigarette on the park bench
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Bruce Oppenheimer places the performance in Cape Town in the mid or late fifties, perhaps the early sixties; no South African tour of those years is separately documented in the sources reached, and no Cape Town theatre is named. The date is a midpoint of his own stated range.
stops.campa: Somewhere in the Cape Town of the later fifties he does the thing that one man in the audience is still describing sixty years later. Halfway through the second act he pulls down a screen with the words of Wu nehmt men a bissele mazel printed on it, sings it through once with the house, then sits on the stage park bench and lights a cigarette while the house sings it for him. The gag is that he is doing nothing at all, in front of a full theatre, and the nothing is the performance. The witness cannot fix the year closer than the mid or late fifties, perhaps the early sixties, and names no Cape Town theatre.
stops.quote: I saw him in Cape Town in the mid or late fifties and perhaps early sixties. I remember one part very clearly. In the second half of the play, after the audience was warmed up, he pulled down a sort of screen with the words of 'Wu nehmt men a bissele mazel,' and after singing it once with the audience, he sat down on a park bench on stage, lit a cigarette, while the audience sang, with heavy pathos. I recall his sangfroid..., the insouciance, the chutzpa, that he should be having a break and having a smoke.
stops.quote_source: Bruce Oppenheimer, recollection to Veronica Belling, quoted in Belling, Digital Yiddish Theatre Project, 2020
suggested_refs: The song 'Wu nehmt men a bissele mazel' and its use as an audience number

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Odeon session
stops.date_confidence: The Argentine Boletin Oficial of 21 and 27 August 1957 registers two Spanish-language compositions credited to Max Perelman, words and music, issued by Odeon in Buenos Aires in October 1956, in a pressing of 300 copies. The day is not given. The Boletin does not state the genre of either song and they should not be called tangos on this evidence. The studio address is not recorded, so the pin is the generic Buenos Aires coordinate.
stops.campa: He records two songs of his own, in Spanish, for Odeon: No es como se quiere and Dinero y mas dinero. The Argentine state registry logs the pressing the following year at three hundred copies. Money and more money: the title is the subject of half his Buenos Aires repertoire, sung by a man whose audience arrived with nothing and counted every peso in a language they were still assembling out of Yiddish and Spanish at once. Three hundred discs is not fame. It is a document. The Boletin Oficial states no genre for either side, so neither song can be called a tango on this evidence.
suggested_refs: Odeon disc, Buenos Aires, October 1956: 'No es como se quiere' / 'Dinero y mas dinero'; registration in the Boletin Oficial, 21 and 27 August 1957
sources: Boletin Oficial de la Republica Argentina, 2da seccion, 21 August 1957
Boletin Oficial de la Republica Argentina, 2da seccion, 27 August 1957

stops.name: Haifa, the mass circuit
stops.date_confidence: Belling describes an extensive Israeli touring circuit across the 1950s and 1960s taking in Haifa, Tiberias, Netanya, Nahariya, Afula and the towns of the Emek Yizrael; no theatre and no year is fixed for any one of them. Haifa stands here for the whole circuit and the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: For most of two decades the company works the country outside the two big cities: Haifa, Tiberias, Netanya, Nahariya, Afula, the immigrant towns of the valley. These are not the houses the national theatre plays. The audience is the mass Yiddish-speaking immigration, and the reviews that matter to him are not written down. One is, though. A member of Habima, the Hebrew national company, watches him work and reports back on it with an honesty the purists in the press never manage.
stops.quote: the popular Yiddish performer ... connected with his audience, and that he [the Habima actor] himself laughed at his jokes.
stops.quote_source: Unnamed member of the Habima theatre, quoted in Belling, Digital Yiddish Theatre Project, 2020; the ellipsis is in the source
suggested_refs: The Israeli provincial touring circuit of the 1950s and 1960s

stops.name: Tel Aviv-Jaffa, the poster for Oy! Vayber Vayber!
stops.date_confidence: Date and title read from a surviving poster in the National Library of Israel's ephemera catalogue, record NNL_EPHEMERA997000980890405171. The poster gives the Tel Aviv-Jaffa area but the specific hall is not established from the catalogue record, so the pin is the city coordinate.
stops.campa: A poster survives, which is more than survives of most of what he did. It advertises Max Perlman and troupe in Oy! Vayber Vayber! in the Tel Aviv-Jaffa area on the eleventh of December. The sheet was printed to be pasted up and torn down inside a week, and paper of exactly that kind is what carries the evidence of a career built on nights nobody recorded. Thirteen more bearing his name turn up decades later in a Stanford collection of eighty-one Israeli Yiddish entertainment posters. The hall is not established from the catalogue record, so the pin is the city.
suggested_refs: National Library of Israel ephemera record NNL_EPHEMERA997000980890405171; the Stanford collection of eighty-one Israeli Yiddish entertainment posters, early 1930s to 1981
sources: National Library of Israel ephemera catalogue
Digital Yiddish Theatre Project, 'Wikidata, Yiddish Theatre Posters, and the World'

segments.name: The New York Years, and Two Returns to Buenos Aires

stops.name: Roosevelt Theater, New York, Honeymoon in Israel
stops.date_confidence: The production and the theatre name are firm: the New York Times reviewed it on 15 October 1962 as 'Theater: Yiddish Musical: Honeymoon in Israel at the Roosevelt'. The theatre's address is NOT established. The Roosevelt on East Houston Street that ran Yiddish programming closed in 1951 and was demolished in 1959, and the Harlem Roosevelt is a different house; the earlier attribution of this stop to Second Avenue is unsupported and the coordinate should be treated as a placeholder in the East Village rather than a location.
stops.campa: At fifty-three he opens on the New York Yiddish stage for the first time, in Honeymoon in Israel at a theatre called the Roosevelt whose street address nobody has been able to establish since. The same year the song Kh'vil nisht keyn sakh nor a bisele, words and music his own, is published: I don't want much, just a little. The New York Times, which will review him five times over twenty-two years, files him immediately under the two things it will never stop mentioning.
stops.quote: an engaging comedian, who uses a hat and a tremendous smile as props
stops.quote_source: New York Times, quoted in Belling, Digital Yiddish Theatre Project, 2020; the production is not specified in the source
suggested_refs: 'Kh'vil nisht keyn sakh nor a bisele,' words and music by Max Perlman, published 1962; Workers Circle Mlotek Yiddish Song Collection
sources: Workers Circle Mlotek Yiddish Song Collection

stops.name: Roosevelt Theater, New York, Don't Worry, Brother
stops.date_confidence: Belling dates the production to 1963 and the two New York Times lines quoted about it to the same year; no opening date is recorded. The coordinate carries the same unresolved address problem as the 1962 stop and is a placeholder.
stops.campa: He returns to the Roosevelt the following season in Don't Worry, Brother, and the New York Times returns with him. It calls the evening a comfortable evening of familiar horseplay, which is not praise and is not quite an insult either. Two seasons in the same house, and the address of the house is one of the things about him that has simply been lost. Then the same notice turns to the performer and concedes in a single clause everything the rest of it is trying to withhold. The hat again.
stops.quote: the agile, beaming star, who uses his hat as an indispensable prop, and knows how to find rapport with the audience.
stops.quote_source: New York Times on Don't Worry, Brother at the Roosevelt Theater, 1963, quoted in Belling, Digital Yiddish Theatre Project, 2020
suggested_refs: The New York Times notices of the Roosevelt Theater Yiddish seasons, 1962-1963

stops.name: Anderson Yiddish Theater, 66 Second Avenue, Good Luck
stops.date_confidence: Cast and production details from the NYU Second Avenue Online programme holdings as cited by Belling; the address of the Anderson at 66 Second Avenue is independently documented. No opening date is recorded and the month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: On Second Avenue proper now, at the Anderson, he plays Yosel Soloveitchik in Good Luck to music by Sholem Secunda, with Miriam Kressyn, Jacob Jacobs, Fyvush Finkel, Seymour Rexite, and Gita Galina as Zisel. Secunda, who wrote Bei Mir Bistu Shein, also set one of his lyrics, Zol es geyn vi es geyt. It is the densest Yiddish-theatre company he ever stands in the middle of, and it stands on Second Avenue in the decade the street stops being able to fill its houses. The Anderson is at number 66. The programme survives in the NYU holdings; no opening date does.
suggested_refs: The Anderson Theater, 66 Second Avenue; NYU Second Avenue Online programme archive
sources: NYU Second Avenue Online programme holdings
Robert and Molly Freedman Jewish Sound Archive, University of Pennsylvania

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the 1966 return
stops.date_confidence: The UBA dictionary records Argentine return engagements in 1955, 1966 and 1967. No venue, month or production is given for 1966, and the pin is the generic Buenos Aires coordinate.
stops.campa: He comes back to Buenos Aires again, twenty-seven years after the Oceania. Nothing is recorded of what he played or where. The dictionary of exiled Jewish musicians in Argentina lists the year in a sequence of three, 1955, 1966, 1967, and moves on. He is fifty-seven, and the Yiddish houses of Corrientes are closing one after another. He reached this city by accident in 1939, running from a war. He keeps coming back to it now that he no longer has to.
suggested_refs: The Argentine return engagements of 1955, 1966 and 1967
sources: Glocer et al., Diccionario, vol. II, p. 157

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the tour with Shimon Dzigan
stops.date_confidence: Belling names the Dzigan pairing; the UBA dictionary independently confirms an Argentine engagement in 1967. A Brazilian leg attached to this tour in some accounts is not supported by either source and is not staged here. No venue is named.
stops.campa: He tours Argentina with Shimon Dzigan, the great comedian of Lodz, survivor of the Soviet camps, the last enormous name of Eastern European Yiddish comedy. The two personas are set against each other on the same bill: Dzigan carrying the old country in the bones of his delivery, Perelman urbane, cocksure, hatted, a man from nowhere in particular who can work a room in five languages. The Buenos Aires audience of 1967 is old enough to recognise both of them as its own.
suggested_refs: Shimon Dzigan's South American tours of the 1960s
sources: Glocer et al., Diccionario, vol. II, p. 157

stops.name: Actors' Playhouse, Seventh Avenue South, Never Too Late for Happiness
stops.date_confidence: Venue and cast from the NYU Second Avenue Online holdings and Belling; the title is Belling's form, Never Too Late for Happiness. A description of it as a remake of The Lithuanian Yankee circulates but does not appear in her text and is unsourced. Coordinate corrected to the OSM geocode of 100 Seventh Avenue South. No opening date is recorded.
stops.campa: Downtown, in Greenwich Village rather than on Second Avenue, he plays Never Too Late for Happiness with Galina, Leon Liebgold, Jacob Jacobs and Fraydele Oysher. The Actors' Playhouse at 100 Seventh Avenue South is an off-Broadway house and never was a Yiddish theatre, which is where the language has got to by 1968. The company is by now a repertory of survivors performing to survivors in rooms built for other purposes. Liebgold has been playing leading men since Warsaw before the war. Oysher sings.
suggested_refs: Actors' Playhouse, 100 Seventh Avenue South, New York
sources: NYU Second Avenue Online programme holdings

stops.name: Anderson Yiddish Theater, Oh What a Wedding!
stops.date_confidence: Belling names the production, the composer Murray Rumshinsky and the lyricist Jacob Jacobs, and dates it 1969; no opening date is recorded.
stops.campa: Back at the Anderson for Oh What a Wedding!, music by Murray Rumshinsky, lyrics by Jacob Jacobs. Rumshinsky's father wrote for Second Avenue when the street had a dozen houses on it; the son is writing for its last two. Galina is sixty-two and the ingenue parts have passed to Menora Zahav, who has been working beside him since she was fifteen in Johannesburg. Galina does not leave the company. She simply plays the other roles, and the two of them go on sharing a billing they have shared since Riga.
suggested_refs: Oh What a Wedding!, Anderson Yiddish Theater, 1969

segments.name: Late Seasons: Jerusalem, Johannesburg, Town Hall

stops.name: Jerusalem, the Mitchell Theatre, with the Prime Minister in the stalls
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The whole of the evidence is Bruce Oppenheimer's recollection to Belling, which places the performance at the Mitchell Theatre in Jerusalem around 1971 or 1972 with Golda Meir in the audience. No programme, press notice or security record has been produced. The venue's address was not independently located and the pin is the Jerusalem city coordinate.
stops.campa: In a Jerusalem theatre one night the Prime Minister of Israel comes in after the lights are down, with a thin detail, and takes a seat in the stalls to watch a Yiddish comedy. The state has spent two decades discouraging exactly this. The man onstage is sixty-two and has been doing the same act, refined, since Riga. Meir was born in Kiev and Yiddish was her first language, as it was the first language of most of the room. The only witness on record is a young man sitting one row behind her.
stops.quote: I sat upstairs and I recall that Golda Meir who was Prime Minister at the time, came in after lights out, with a meagre security detail and sat in front of me. I was so excited and happy to be in the same space as her, watching Yiddish theatre.
stops.quote_source: Bruce Oppenheimer, recollection to Veronica Belling, quoted in Belling, Digital Yiddish Theatre Project, 2020
suggested_refs: The Mitchell Theatre, Jerusalem, c. 1971-1972

stops.name: Johannesburg, the last South African tour
stops.date_confidence: The 1972 return is attested through Chaim Lewis's review in Jewish Affairs of May 1972, cited by Belling. The itinerary is not broken down city by city, and Johannesburg stands for the tour.
stops.campa: Twenty-four years after the first season at His Majesty's he comes back to South Africa, sixty-three years old, and the critic Chaim Lewis watches him with the eye of someone who has seen him before. A quarter of a century later the Mail and Guardian will file him among the largely forgotten names that South African Jews nonetheless remember with great warmth. Lewis is not writing about a play. He is writing about a technique, and he finds a verb for it that nobody else in fifty years of notices thought of.
stops.quote: an artist to his fingertips—he snake charms the audiences. The measure of his magic are the smiling faces of the audience.
stops.quote_source: Chaim Lewis, Jewish Affairs, May 1972, quoted in Belling, Digital Yiddish Theatre Project, 2020
suggested_refs: Chaim Lewis, review in Jewish Affairs, May 1972
sources: Mail & Guardian, 'Oy, what a drama!', 18 April 1997

stops.name: Norman Thomas Theater, East 33rd Street, Dem shmids tekhter
stops.date_confidence: Belling dates the production to October 1981 at the Norman Thomas Theater, in the auditorium of Norman Thomas High School on East 33rd Street; no opening day is given.
stops.campa: At seventy-two he plays an old grandfather in Peretz Hirshbein's The Blacksmith's Daughters, in a production associated with Ben Bonus and Mina Bern, staged in a high school auditorium on East 33rd Street. It is a literary Yiddish play, the kind the kultur-menshn of Johannesburg in 1948 accused him of never doing. The house is a school auditorium with the seats bolted to the floor. He plays the part straight. The New York Times, reviewing the evening, reaches for a compliment that keeps one foot in the kitchen.
stops.quote: tasteful and tasty, light as a matzoh ball, yet embodying the bucolic and artistic flavour so deftly imparted by Hirshbein
stops.quote_source: New York Times, 1981 review of Dem shmids tekhter, quoted in Belling, Digital Yiddish Theatre Project, 2020
suggested_refs: Peretz Hirshbein, Dem shmids tekhter; the Norman Thomas High School auditorium, East 33rd Street

stops.name: Holon Cemetery, burying Gita Galina
stops.date_confidence: Belling gives leukemia, burial at Holon, and a death roughly two and a half years before Max's own. The precise date of 6 January 1983 comes from Wikidata Q81939577 citing BillionGraves cemetery data, which has not been checked against the gravestone itself. The coordinate is the OSM geocode for Holon Cemetery, correcting an earlier value 3.2 km to the north-east.
stops.campa: Gita Galina dies of leukemia and is buried in the cemetery at Holon. They had been on the same playbill since Riga in the early thirties: Vienna, Paris, Whitechapel, the Oceania, Corrientes, Johannesburg, the Grand Palais, Second Avenue. He is seventy-three and has never worked a career she was not in. The date on her record comes from a photograph of the gravestone; her own file gives Vitebsk, 1907, a birth name of Guta Israiley, and this ground. His, when it comes, will give less than that. He goes on touring for two more years.
suggested_refs: The graves of Gita Galina and Max Perlman, Holon cemetery

stops.name: Town Hall, West 43rd Street, Oy Mama! Am I in Love
stops.date_confidence: Belling names Town Hall for the last New York tour with the Shalom Yiddish Musical Comedy Theatre; a UBA-derived note in circulation names a different venue for the same production and the discrepancy is not resolved here. No opening date is recorded.
stops.campa: His last New York engagement, at Town Hall on West 43rd Street, with the Shalom Yiddish Musical Comedy Theatre in Oy Mama! Am I in Love. He is seventy-five and a widower. Town Hall is not a Yiddish theatre and never was; it is a concert hall hired for the night, because the houses that were built for this are gone. The Times reviewer, filing on a form of theatre with almost no rooms left in the city, spends his best line not on the star but on the woman playing opposite him. It is the last time the name goes up in New York.
stops.quote: the redoubtable and decidedly charming comedienne
stops.quote_source: New York Times, 1984, on Mary Soreano, Perlman's co-star in Oy Mama! Am I in Love, quoted in Belling, Digital Yiddish Theatre Project, 2020
suggested_refs: Town Hall, 123 West 43rd Street; the Shalom Yiddish Musical Comedy Theatre

segments.name: The Last Tour and the Ground at Holon

stops.name: Sydney, the final tour
stops.date_confidence: Belling names Sydney as the Australian city of the final tour. The UBA dictionary is wider: 'Hizo sus ultimas actuaciones en 1985 en gira por Estados Unidos, Australia e Israel con su companera Menorah Zahav.' The tour therefore took in the United States and Israel as well; no Sydney theatre is named and no dates are given for any leg.
stops.campa: The last tour runs through the United States, Australia and Israel, with Menora Zahav, who first stood on a stage with him in Johannesburg in 1951 at fifteen and a half. Sydney is the far end of it, as far from Riga as a working actor can get. It is booked the way every tour has been booked since 1934: a company, a repertoire, a series of halls, a return ticket. He is seventy-six. He comes off the Australian leg exhausted in a way that is not the ordinary exhaustion of a tour, and he flies home.
suggested_refs: The 1985 farewell tour of the United States, Australia and Israel with Menora Zahav
sources: Glocer et al., Diccionario, vol. II, p. 157

stops.name: Israel, the diagnosis on returning
stops.date_confidence: Belling reports the diagnosis of advanced terminal cancer on his return from Australia, without a date, a type, a hospital or a city. June 1985 is chosen only to sit between the tour and the death of 23 July. The pin is the general Tel Aviv coordinate; the place of diagnosis is not established anywhere.
stops.campa: Back in Israel the exhaustion is examined and found to be cancer, already at its final stage. He had been onstage within the year, in three countries, at seventy-six, with a hat. The record of a man who spent seven decades in front of audiences goes quiet at exactly the point where a modern life usually leaves its thickest paper. No source names the disease. No source names the hospital. No source names the city. Belling reports the diagnosis with no date attached to it, and the next fixed point in the record is the twenty-third of July.
suggested_refs: The undocumented final illness: no hospital, city or diagnosis named in any reachable source

stops.name: Holon Cemetery, buried beside her
stops.date_confidence: The day and month rest on Belling alone. Wikidata Q81939428 carries only the year 1985 and records no place of death and no place of burial at all, despite holding VIAF, Library of Congress, WorldCat, Google Knowledge Graph and Zemereshet identifiers for him; it cannot be cited as corroboration for 23 July.
stops.campa: He dies in Israel on the twenty-third of July and is buried at Holon beside Gita Galina, two and a half years after her. The authority record that carries his name in five international catalogues does not know where he is buried or where he died. What is left above ground is thirteen posters in a Stanford collection, one Warsaw film from 1938, an Odeon disc of three hundred copies, a shelf of songs in an archive in Philadelphia, and a phrase a critic in Johannesburg found for him in 1972: he snake charms the audiences.
suggested_refs: Holon cemetery, the joint grave; the Freedman Jewish Sound Archive artist file; Karsten Troyke's revivals of 'Ven Du Lakhst' (2006) and of 'Glik,' 'Ahava,' 'Vus Geven Iz Geshen' and 'Alts Tsilib Parnusse' (2012)
sources: Robert and Molly Freedman Jewish Sound Archive, University of Pennsylvania
Internet Archive, 'At the Yiddish Theatre' (Greater Recording Co. GRC-216, 1971)
